instructor:
Prof. Aytür is an outstandingly knowledgable, sympathetic and equally busy person. It is obvious that he is very much into his field of study and you can feel it in the class. He is a very good communicator who is concise and speaks carefully, but the problem is that once you zone out for a couple of seconds, because of his precision, there is no leeway to join back into the topic and focus on his train of thought, because by the time you're processing what he said, he already spoke one or two (carefully selected and information-filled) sentences which covered the entire curriculum and you have probably missed something essential to the topic of conversation. It is a good idea to listen to all classes carefully, but with his classes, it is more than a necessity; it is equally rewarding when you understand what he says.

His notetaking and scriptural ability are extremely high, his notes are very clear and whiteboard usage is very good; all notes are written down on the whiteboard (plus anything that may come up in the classroom), but I think he gets distracted too quickly between topics and sometimes loses coherence. It is not uncommon that a topic is covered before and/or after a brief introduction to another topic in full detail. I think this is due to his personal preference of seeing his topic as different patterns of thought connected together through a very good understanding of his field, but it is an unaccustomed, non-linear, type of learning for most students. However, I overall think this has a positive effect on student learning. I have thoroughly enjoyed his class and would recommend taking classes from him. He can be demanding at times when it comes to the coursework but he has never said anything negative that I would look at his classes in distaste in hindsight and that is a very commendable, rare quality.
course:
This class might be somewhat manageable for a student with an extra interest in optics or students with an EEE / Physics background, but it is extremely taxing for students with minimal exposure to common concepts in signals & systems and electric fields. The curriculum is similar to most other Optics classes in different universities in and outside of Turkey, but the explanations and the general flow of the class are completely unique to most other classes that I was able to reach the notes for on the internet. The only textbook that somewhat overlaps with the curriculum of this class, A. Saleh & M. Teich - Fundamentals of Photonics (2019) is a terrible, terrible resource for self-learning because the most important derivations and ideas are omitted, therefore your only choice is to follow instructor notes most of the time, luckily Prof. Aytür shares notes with the students but of course, they are limited because they can't capture everything said within the classroom.

This class also has a mandatory lab which is very engaging, teaches new concepts, as well as lets you get your hands dirty with some real experience in laser optics. The problem is that most topics of the lab are outside the classroom, by which I mean that the class itself is highly theoretical while part of the laboratory duty deals with real-world experience and explanation of physical phenomena, which means it's also a job and a half on top of your normal responsibilities: It takes easily more than 3-4 hours at some weeks which means if you live off-campus, you will most likely miss the last shuttle to your home. The prelab derivations are mandatory for some work and are sometimes challenging, but they are guaranteed to take a couple more hours of your time.

I overall think this was an extremely productive and enlightening class, but if you have too much coursework already, you won't be able to keep up with the responsibilities of this course as it requires perpetual learning.
